en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Elder Sumati, also titled *The Assembly Before All Buddhas*, and further titled *The Manifestation Taught by the Tathāgata for the Sake of Sentient Beings*.
Translated by the Layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi during the Wu Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with...
The great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus was together with him.
At that time, when it was time, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city for alms together with Ānanda.
At that time, there was a son of a great elder in the city named Sumati.

When this man passed away, his parents, kinsmen, and all his acquaintances simultaneously wailed and wept; they lamented with grief, leaping up and down, crying out in resentment and calling for help, until they fainted upon the ground.
Some called out for their parents and brothers, while others called for their husbands or masters; thus they wailed and wept in various ways.

Furthermore, there were those who took up earth and smeared it over themselves, and others who took up knives to cut off their hair; they were like people with poisoned arrows lodged in their hearts, suffering immeasurable pain and distress.

Some covered themselves with their robes and wept in grief, like a great wind fanning and tossing forest trees so that their branches strike one another, or like fish deprived of water, writhing upon the ground.
Furthermore, it was as if a great tree had been felled and lay in a heap of wreckage;
such agonizing torment was inflicted upon his body.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
“Ānanda! For what reason are that great assembly wailing and weeping so piteously?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In this city there was a son of a great elder named Sumati, who has reached the end of his lifespan and passed away.
Because his parents, brothers, wife, children, kinsmen, and friends are bound by the ties of affection, they are thus deluded and distraught.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, for the sake of delivering all beings, will go there.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not preach without being requested.
I now entreat the Buddha, the World-Honored One, on behalf of those people; out of great compassion, I pray that you will go there."
At that time, the Tathāgata accepted Ānanda’s invitation and proceeded directly to his home.
Then, seeing the World-Honored One from afar, those people each wiped their faces with their hands and came forward to welcome the Buddha.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet; overcome with grief and choked with sobs, he was unable to speak.
Just as he wished to let out a long sigh, because of his reverence for the Buddha, he did not dare to exhale, remaining there holding his breath.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elder’s parents, brothers, kinsmen, and acquaintances:
"Why do you weep and lament, clinging to these illusory phenomena?"
Then all these people simultaneously raised their voices and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Among those in this city, there is only this man who is intelligent and wise, handsome and extraordinary, and being in the prime of his youth, he is unsurpassed among all men."
We constantly think of him, never departing from our hearts; all people look up to him, never wearying of the sight.
His speech is gentle and mild; he is filial toward his parents and respectful and obedient toward his brothers.
Furthermore, he possesses abundant wealth and treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, and amber—his storehouses overflow, and he is fully endowed with precious gems.
Furthermore, we possess carriages, horses, food and drink, medicine, clothing, bedding, servants, and laborers;
all such things are fully provided. Yet, in a single day, our lives have come to an end. For this reason, we weep with grief and long for you so intensely that we cannot restrain ourselves.
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
We pray that you will skillfully expound the Dharma for our sake, so that we may be freed from all afflictions and never again undergo such sufferings as these from this day forward.
One attains the severance of the roots of all fetters—greed, hatred, and delusion;
one attains the crossing to the further shore beyond birth, aging, sickness, and death;
and one is forever liberated from the ocean of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"In whatever place he is born, may he encounter the Buddhas, meet with spiritual friends, and never encounter adverse conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the parents, kinsmen, acquaintances, and the great assembly of the elder:
"Have you ever seen anyone who was born and yet did not grow old, did not fall ill, and did not die?"
Those people said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
We have never seen such a thing.”
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"If you wish to be free from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, do not again harbor thoughts of the bonds of affection and love;
fix your minds on right view and take refuge in the Triple Gem."
Why is this so? Because among all those in the world, there is none who surpasses the Buddha; he alone is able to guide the masses who are blind, ignorant, and deluded.
Among all caravan leaders and kings of physicians, none possesses the marks and signs equal to those of the Buddha.
Why is this so? Because the body of the Tathāgata is the King of Medicine, and the Dharma taught by the Buddha is the excellent medicine.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In the worlds of the ten directions, there is none among the born who does not die;
regarding the path of birth, death, and transmigration, only the Dharma can extinguish it.
There is no land in the ten directions that can save one at the end of life."
"Only the Buddha can sever and eliminate it; therefore, I take refuge in the Buddha.
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"How do you understand what is called death?"
The people replied,
“We do not know,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, envy, anger, and delusion—if a person commits these ten unwholesome deeds, it is called death."
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"If a person is rebellious and does not obey their parents, does not practice the True Dharma, and does not respect śramaṇas, brahmins, and the elders—such a person is also said to be dead."
He further addressed the great assembly:
"If there are those who do not revere the Triple Gem and the śramaṇas who uphold the precepts and possess virtue, such persons are also said to be dead."
He further addressed the great assembly:
"If there are those who are stingy, greedy, jealous, or arrogant; who do not maintain the precepts themselves, nor do their family members—whether elders or juniors—maintain them either;
whose speech is coarse and evil, and who delight in harming others;"
They are deranged and deluded, indolent, and their minds are restless;
their six sense faculties are incomplete, they possess little wisdom,
they cannot maintain focused correctness, and they are prone to trusting the words of others.
Constantly harboring envy and anger while praising oneself;
obstructing the virtues of others and broadcasting their faults;
delighting in self-exaltation and being unable to draw near to śramaṇas or brahmins, thus failing to hear the True Dharma—such a person is also said to be dead.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If a person commits unwholesome deeds, Delighting in the practice of the ten evils,
Their mind constantly harbors arrogance, And they show no reverence for the Triple Gem."
Those who cannot maintain pure precepts, who are indolent and lack diligence—
all such persons as these are said to be dead.
Those who delight in committing various evils will fall into the evil realms upon rebirth.
If a person practices various virtues, they shall then be born in heaven.
If a person does not believe in the Buddha, nor practices the Dharma,
but instead acts contrary to the Dharma— this is what is called death.

He further addressed the great assembly: "If a person attains wealth and status yet remains free from arrogance, their mind is always peaceful and joyful; they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others, treating all with an impartial heart as they would themselves. Though they have attained wealth and status, their mind remains unchanged; they constantly contemplate impermanence and do not regard things as their own, viewing them as more dangerous than a poisonous enemy. They understand that all phenomena must inevitably undergo separation."
Having understood this, one should practice with diligent effort;
knowing that all phenomena have nothing upon which to rely, one does not conceive of fame or profit as "mine," nor does one become attached to any sensory objects;
one constantly cultivates the mind and draws near to those who possess wisdom.
"Do not associate with evil friends, but always seek to remain far removed from them;
as for the Dharma taught by the Buddha, never let it be lost or neglected at the outset.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Rare are those beings, dwelling in this world, who attain great wealth and status yet remain free from arrogance.
Those who practice arrogance cannot escape suffering; if they are not arrogant, they will swiftly attain liberation."
Those who are free from pride will certainly attain liberation; those who possess pride will surely fall into the evil realms.
To sever pride is not called death; to possess pride is what is called death.
He further addressed the great assembly:
"Do you know that there is birth, old age, sickness, and death; that the spirit transmigrates through this life and future lives, repeatedly receiving new forms?"
The people replied,
“We do not know, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"You should know this!
Sentient beings are bound by these four causes and conditions; their spirits revolve through the five realms of existence, unaware of where they come from when born or where they go when they die."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To perceive the impermanent as permanent, To perceive the impure as pure,
To speak of suffering as pleasure, And to perceive the non-self as self."
Within the cycle of birth and death, sentient beings are deeply attached to inverted views;
throughout kalpas numbering in the thousands of myriads of koṭis, they do not know the root of birth and death.
If there is anyone who can understand this true and great Dharma, [they shall attain liberation].
To be able to know that this is impermanent is the foremost root of great suffering.
If a person perceives the defilements and cuts off the roots of the three poisons,
they will surely be able to achieve the unsurpassed Great Dharma.
He further addressed the great assembly:
"Because of the fetters and afflictions, various causes and conditions arise;
because of these causes and conditions, one undergoes all manner of suffering and distress."
For this reason, one revolves through birth and death.
Form does not go to a future life; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not go to a future life. Why is this so?
"The five aggregates are unattainable, not solid, and do not endure for even a moment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Due to the various fetters and afflictions, The causes and conditions for manifold evils arise."
For these causes and conditions, one undergoes immeasurable suffering.
Because of undergoing such sufferings, one further gives rise to immeasurable fetters;
this is the root of all birth and death, and the cycle of transmigration is entirely like this.
All the beautiful forms in the world are like foam upon the water;
All manifold sufferings are likened to rain bubbles;
All manifold perceptions are no different from a mirage.
All immeasurable conditioned phenomena, their nature is like the plantain tree;
all mental consciousnesses are like illusions, devoid of reality.
Such is the sublime Dharma spoken from the mouth of the Tathāgata.
"The sublime Dharma of all Buddhas has already been expounded for you;
out of compassion for sentient beings, I have preached this nectar-like Dharma.
He further addressed the great assembly:
"Earth does not go to future lives; water, fire, and wind likewise do not go to future lives.
Why is this? Earth has no sensation and no cognition;
the four great elements are without consciousness. Earth is a deceptive construct formed by the combination of the four great elements; for these reasons, it does not go to future lives."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Among all phenomena, there is no form and no color;
there is also nothing to be perceived, for they are illusory and lack any reality."
"Composed of the four great elements through provisional combination, it is supple and lacks any solidity.
To wish for it to reach a future life—such a thing is ultimately impossible.
He further addressed the great assembly:
"The eye does not go on to a future life; nor do the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind go on to a future life.
Why is this? Because the eye is empty, without self, impermanent, and lacks even momentary stability."

Even if one wishes to cause them to cease, it cannot be done; they arise when conditions are present and perish when conditions disperse. Their arising comes from nowhere, and their passing goes nowhere;
the same is true for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
All you people, you should know!
These six sense-faculties exist when conditions assemble and cease to exist when conditions disperse;
they are like guests who cannot remain for long.

Furthermore, it is like a person in debt who calculates the days to repay their obligation; once the day is finished, they depart, and there is ultimately no fixed time for them to remain. Upon departing, they become empty and can never be found again, having neither coming nor going.
These six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are likewise thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The various sense-faculties are not solid; These phenomena are like space.
They are unstable and devoid of life, And cannot be made into 'mine'."
"Because of causes and conditions there is utility, yet ultimately nothing is fixed.
Phenomena produced through combination cannot be found as they transmigrate through the world.

When the Buddha preached this sutra, three hundred bhikṣus exhausted their outflows and were liberated from their fetters, attaining the path of Arhatship; five hundred devas became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and furthermore, eight thousand devas and humans all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"You all should contemplate impermanence and never depart from this mindfulness.
O great assembly!..."
I know that the Buddhas of the past acted as great bridges for all sentient beings; they possessed great compassion, which extended universally to all.
These Buddhas of the past were named Kāśyapa Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, and Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

All such Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have severed all unwholesome dharmas and cultivated and accumulated profound and immeasurable wholesome dharmas; yet, though they were unimpeded regarding all phenomena, they were all impermanent.
In the past, there were also immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas who delighted in tranquility and skillfully cultivated their minds; yet they too were impermanent.

The disciples of the Buddhas of the past were immeasurable and boundless; they all attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind, as well as the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, forever departing from birth and death to reach the other shore, yet they too were subject to the transformations of impermanence.
In the past, there were also rishis possessing the five supernormal powers who purely cultivated their precepts and lived for immeasurable kalpas, yet they all returned to impermanence.
In ancient times, there were also immeasurable wheel-turning sage kings and various minor kings who possessed the seven treasures in full, lacking nothing, yet they too were impermanent.

In the past, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I served as various kings and practiced universal giving, offering my head, eyes, marrow, and brain, as well as my hands, feet, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, palaces, towers, and all manner of instruments for the five pleasures.
At that time, I concurrently cultivated pure precepts without any deficiency; if anyone came seeking these various things, I gave them with joy, giving rise to neither anger nor envy;
I was courageous and diligent, with body and mind never lax;
and I deeply cultivated meditative concentration, liberation, and samādhi.
With profound and sharp wisdom, vast wisdom, and unimpeded, peerless, and most profound wisdom, he was endowed with such immeasurable merits.
When I was practicing the bodhisattva path, by virtue of these merits, I sat beneath the Bodhi tree and made this vow with a diamond-like mind:

"I shall not rise from this seat until I have conquered the four Māras and attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikadharma*)."

As soon as this thought arose, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, leading his hosts with weapons arrayed and adorned, surrounded the Bodhi tree for thirty-two yojanas on each side and conceived an evil intent:
"With these armies, I shall surely destroy this man and prevent him from attaining the Way."
At that time, I extended my hand and pressed upon the earth; the host of Māra’s followers was immediately shattered and dispersed.
The Dharma that I know, that I have attained, and that I have awakened to shall now manifest its verification, and I shall surely achieve the Way.

At that time, having immediately accumulated immeasurable merit and wisdom, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, and turns the wheel of Dharma; thus, one achieves fulfillment for oneself and likewise brings all sentient beings to fulfillment.
At that time, there were three yakṣas:
the first was named Ārāvaṇa, the second Viśanaga, and the third Śūciloma.
He thus transformed immeasurable spirits and deities such as these, causing them to uphold the precepts.

Among the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths, he is the most honored, the most supreme, and without equal; having severed the very roots of the three poisons, he is free from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and has attained the realization of the unsurpassed Dharma.
"Nevertheless, I too must be turned by impermanence; three months hence, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
He further addressed the great assembly:
"Observe this impermanence; it never forsakes anyone."

Although the Tathāgata has attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and is fully endowed with the marks and signs of the physical body (rūpakāya-lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), he cannot escape [death];
likewise, the Buddhas of the past, future, and present also return to impermanence.
Therefore, you should deeply contemplate the nature of impermanence!

If you can do so, you will no longer harbor hearts of attachment or longing for loved ones, nor will you have thoughts of greed, hatred, or delusion. You will forever sever the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, attain liberation from all unwholesome dharmas, increase immeasurable pure practices, and profoundly penetrate the twelvefold chain of dependent origination of all phenomena.
By these causes and conditions, one constantly encounters the Buddhas. Why is this?
If a person attains penetration into the twelve links of dependent origination, that is itself the seeing of the Dharma.
"One who sees the Dharma is said to see the Buddha;
those who wish to see the Buddha should maintain pure precepts, with their dignified conduct free from deficiency.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The kings of the past, though raised in deep palaces, were heroic, majestic, and handsome,
adorned with every ornament; possessing elephants, horses, chariots, and abundant wealth and treasures—
yet even such kings as these returned to impermanence."
Clad in deerskin garments, Devadatta and other great seers were thoroughly proficient in the scriptures of the non-Buddhist outsiders;
yet even such sages as these have succumbed to impermanence.
Possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, unattached to the three realms and free from all delusion and desire—
such noble ones, this excellent field of merit, likewise return to impermanence.
Without hearing a single word, he has skillfully severed all fetters; diligent for his own sake, he is a great field of merit.
Like a rhinoceros with a single horn, dwelling alone in the mountain forests, even the Pratyekabuddhas of renowned fame must likewise return to impermanence.
At one time they were dispersed and destroyed; having severed all fetters, they attained the Buddha-way.
Having attained the Way, they turned the wheel of Dharma. Though the Buddhas are thus, they too must return to impermanence.
The Buddhas of the future shall firmly establish sentient beings;
the Buddhas of the present, throughout billions of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—all such Buddhas likewise return to impermanence.
The power of impermanence does not spare the realm of desire, nor the realms of form and formlessness;
it likewise spares neither sages and kings, nor the noble and the lowly, nor even the Buddhas,
Pratyekabuddhas, those in training, and those beyond training.
Without regard for wealth or beauty, and regardless of strength or weakness, even those of great wisdom are held fast by it.
From this one should know that impermanence is the ultimate suffering; therefore, one should seek the True Dharma.
Gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools, with flowers and fruits in full bloom;
kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, as well as head and eyes—giving these all as alms, I dedicate this merit toward seeking the Buddha-way.
In times past, I gave away my hands and feet; through such deeds as these, I cultivated patience.
When a hawk pursued a dove, I cut off my own flesh to ransom it, enduring all manner of pain for the sake of the unsurpassed path.
Having long practiced what is difficult to do, I have defeated the Māra King;
beneath the tree of the site of enlightenment, I attained the Way of the Buddha, free from all defilements.
I now turn the Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park.
I have already subdued the Yakṣa of Anger, who dwells among the seven mountains and resides upon the Snowy Mountains.
I have subdued him along with his retinue, yet I am unable to subdue the power of Impermanence.
I am able to subdue them like mountain crags; such fierce elephants, together with their followers, I have all subdued.
Yet there is one power I cannot subdue: the power of impermanence.
"Among all the masters of treatises and the various non-Buddhists,
when I debate with them using the True Dharma, none can surpass me.
I transform sentient beings of other realms and lead them to become my disciples."
Yet I could not subdue the great power of impermanence.
The bonds of self-view and craving, as well as hatred and delusion—
these laws of ignorance have all been eradicated.
Although he lit the great lamp of wisdom to illuminate the trichiliocosm,
he was unable to subdue the mighty power of impermanence;
yet he did conquer the celestial Māra king, along with all his hosts.
He destroys the great blinding darkness and illuminates with the light of the True Dharma.
He also subdues all masters of treatises and all practitioners of divination;
yet he cannot subdue the great power of impermanence.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
You have skillfully analyzed and explained this Dharma.
What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said:
"This sutra is named 'Eliminating All Sorrow and Affliction'; you should receive and uphold it.
It is also named 'Assembled Before All Buddhas,' and it is further named 'What the Tathāgata Has Spoken to Manifest to Sentient Beings'; you should receive and uphold it."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In future ages, if there are good men or good women who receive and uphold this *Sūtra on the Manifestations Taught by the Tathāgata for Sentient Beings*, they shall recognize their own past lives throughout seven births; poisons shall not harm them, fire shall not burn them, and water shall not sweep them away. They shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or the eight difficult conditions.
After casting off this body, they shall be born before Maitreya and attain a place in Maitreya’s first assembly."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Ānanda and the great assembly—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Elder Sumati Spoken by the Buddha
